overview: Visualization is not about making charts look good — it is about thinking. Visualization is a cognitive tool, not an output artifact. It reveals what statistics cannot surface immediately, what models may hide, and what metrics may average away.
This module covers why visualization matters, Matplotlib basics, Seaborn statistical plots, and visualizing model results — essential skills for data exploration and model diagnosis.

topics.title: Why Visualization Matters
theory: Humans are excellent at pattern recognition but poor at interpreting raw numbers. Visualization leverages spatial reasoning, color perception, and shape recognition to see trends, detect outliers, spot relationships, and identify errors.

Visualization appears at every stage: data acquisition (are values realistic?), EDA (what patterns exist?), feature engineering (which features matter?), model evaluation (where does the model fail?), and communication (can insights be trusted?).

Statistics quantifies and aggregates; visualization reveals structure and exposes anomalies. Example: Mean accuracy = 92% hides that one class is failing completely. Without visualization, models can lie convincingly.

Visualization prevents silent failures: data leakage, label imbalance, skewed distributions, train-test contamination. It exposes these early. The cost of skipping visualization is misleading metrics and fragile systems.
visualIntuition: Anscombe's Quartet: four datasets with identical statistics but completely different patterns when visualized.
visualSuggestions: Same metric, different underlying distributions comparison

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Always visualize before modeling
data = np.random.randn(1000)

plt.hist(data, bins=30)
plt.title("Distribution Check")
plt.show()

topics.title: Matplotlib Basics
theory: Matplotlib is fundamental because it is primitive — it gives full control over every visual element. Higher-level libraries (Seaborn, Plotly) sit on top of it and abstract decisions away.
Matplotlib follows a hierarchical model: Figure (canvas) → Axes (coordinate system) → Plot elements. Most confusion comes from mixing Figure and Axes concepts.

Pyplot interface (plt.plot()) is state-based — good for exploration but limited for complex layouts. Object-oriented interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots()) provides explicit control and is preferred for production.

Basic plot types serve different purposes: Line plots for trends/time series, scatter plots for relationships, bar plots for categorical comparison, histograms for distributions. Choose plot based on what question you're answering.
visualIntuition: Figure hierarchy diagram: Figure contains Axes, which contains plot elements, labels, ticks, and legends.
visualSuggestions: Same data shown with different plot types

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y = np.sin(x)

# Object-oriented interface (preferred)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.set_xlabel("X")
ax.set_ylabel("sin(X)")
ax.set_title("Sine Wave")
plt.show()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))

# Line plot
axs[0, 0].plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 2, 3])
axs[0, 0].set_title("Line Plot")

# Scatter plot
axs[0, 1].scatter(np.random.randn(50), np.random.randn(50))
axs[0, 1].set_title("Scatter Plot")

# Bar plot
axs[1, 0].bar(['A', 'B', 'C'], [3, 7, 5])
axs[1, 0].set_title("Bar Plot")

# Histogram
axs[1, 1].hist(np.random.randn(1000), bins=30)
axs[1, 1].set_title("Histogram")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

topics.title: Seaborn Statistical Plots
theory: Matplotlib shows how to draw; Seaborn shows what to draw. Seaborn is built for statistical thinking and dataset-aware visualization. It encodes statistical defaults so users focus on meaning, not mechanics.
Seaborn expects a DataFrame with column names and semantic roles (x, y, hue). Visualization becomes declarative: what varies, what is compared, what is grouped.

Distribution plots (histplot, boxplot, violinplot) reveal spread, skewness, multimodality. Relationship plots (regplot, pairplot) show dependency and correlation. Categorical plots (countplot, barplot) compare groups.

Heatmaps compress large matrices into pattern perception — used for correlation analysis, confusion matrices, feature interactions. Faceting (FacetGrid) enables comparison across subsets without overplotting.
visualIntuition: Seaborn's data-centric model: DataFrame columns map directly to visual properties (x, y, hue, size).

code.content:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load example dataset
df = sns.load_dataset('tips')

# Distribution with KDE
sns.histplot(df['total_bill'], kde=True)
plt.title("Bill Distribution")
plt.show()

# Relationship with regression line
sns.regplot(x='total_bill', y='tip', data=df)
plt.show()

# Categorical comparison
sns.boxplot(x='day', y='total_bill', data=df)
plt.show()

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset('iris')

# Correlation heatmap
corr = df.corr()
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, cmap='coolwarm')
plt.title("Feature Correlations")
plt.show()

# Pairplot for EDA
sns.pairplot(df, hue='species')
plt.show()

topics.title: Visualizing Model Results
theory: Metrics compress behavior into numbers; visualization reveals behavior. A model with high accuracy can still fail on edge cases, be biased, overfit specific regions, and generalize poorly.

Regression diagnostics: Predicted vs Actual plot (perfect predictions on diagonal), Residual plot (reveals non-linearity, heteroscedasticity, missing features), Residual distribution (checks for bias and extreme errors).

Classification diagnostics: Confusion matrix (shows what the model confuses), Probability distribution (reveals overconfidence), ROC curve (threshold-independent performance), Precision-Recall curve (important for imbalanced classes).

Learning curves show bias-variance tradeoff and whether more data helps. Feature importance shows what the model relies on. Never tune hyperparameters before understanding failure modes through visualization.
visualIntuition: Model diagnosis framework: predictions vs reality, error patterns, confidence calibration, failure mode analysis.
visualSuggestions: Residual plot showing structured vs random residuals

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

y_true = np.array([3, -0.5, 2, 7])
y_pred = np.array([2.5, 0.0, 2, 8])
residuals = y_true - y_pred

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

# Predicted vs Actual
axs[0].scatter(y_true, y_pred)
axs[0].plot([min(y_true), max(y_true)], [min(y_true), max(y_true)], 'r--')
axs[0].set_xlabel("Actual")
axs[0].set_ylabel("Predicted")
axs[0].set_title("Predicted vs Actual")

# Residual plot
axs[1].scatter(y_pred, residuals)
axs[1].axhline(0, color='r', linestyle='--')
axs[1].set_xlabel("Predicted")
axs[1].set_ylabel("Residual")
axs[1].set_title("Residual Plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
import numpy as np

y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0])
y_pred = np.array([0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0])

cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues')
plt.xlabel("Predicted")
plt.ylabel("Actual")
plt.title("Confusion Matrix")
plt.show()
